title: SWOT analysis for a small cleaning business
audience: Owners and managers of a small cleaning business, or a business starting up, who need a structured strategy check.
learningOutcomes: Separate internal factors (strengths and weaknesses) from external factors (opportunities and threats)
Support each SWOT item with evidence, or label it as an assumption
Pair SWOT items to choose one action with an owner and a date

instruction.heading: What a SWOT is for
instruction.body: A SWOT analysis sorts the business's situation into four boxes. Strengths and weaknesses sit inside the business, so you can change them. Opportunities and threats come from outside, so you respond to them. The value lies in the actions the analysis leads to. A grid of adjectives that nobody acts on is a poster, not an analysis. Keep each box to about five to seven items, and rank the top three in each.

instruction.heading: Strengths need evidence
instruction.body: The sample plan lists an enthusiastic leader, a training program that records how the business works, and experienced, dedicated staff. Each is a plausible strength, but it only becomes useful when a result shows it. A leader's energy matters less than a completion rate, a complaint rate or a count of repeat bookings. Ask for the measure behind each strength. If none exists, record the strength as an assumption and plan to measure it.

instruction.heading: Weaknesses need a response
instruction.body: The sample names three weaknesses: the industry is labour-intensive, trust takes time to build, and a start-up has little brand recognition. None of these is a reason to stop. Each one needs a response written beside it. Labour intensity points to a pricing approach based on hours and to scheduling that keeps crews productive. Slow trust points to a referral process and early client follow-up. Limited brand recognition points to a consistent and visible standard on every job.

instruction.heading: Opportunities that can be tested
instruction.body: The sample lists a large part of the market that is unaware of the business, a shift away from individual housekeepers, changing consumer habits that favour outsourcing cleaning, and a model that can be scaled. For each one, write which customers it applies to, how many local prospects it describes, and what action it allows. An opportunity you cannot act on this quarter belongs on a later list. The scalability claim, for example, stays a hypothesis until you have a repeatable process and a trained second team.

instruction.heading: Threats and their causes
instruction.body: The sample lists staff turnover and strong competitors. Turnover has causes you can influence: pay, rostering, the quality of induction, supervision and whether people feel their work is valued. Competitors are a threat only when you can name them and compare them. Write down the three nearest competitors by name, what they charge, and where they are weaker than you.

instruction.heading: From grid to action
instruction.body: Pair items to decide what to do. A strength matched with an opportunity suggests a move to pursue, such as a referral offer to a group that already trusts your work. A weakness matched with a threat suggests a protective action, such as a fixed rostering rule that keeps staff. Choose one action from each pairing, give it an owner and a review date, and set the rest aside until the first action is complete.

procedure: Write the four headings and list items under each one.
Attach evidence to each strength and weakness, or mark it as an assumption.
Name the local source or test for each opportunity and threat.
Rank the top three items in each box.
Pair one strength or weakness with one opportunity or threat.
Choose one action per pairing, with an owner and a review date.
Repeat the analysis every six months, or sooner after a major change.

workedExamples.situation: A sole cleaner has strong referrals from two existing clients and has open capacity on weekday mornings. A larger competitor has started offering discounts in the same suburb.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Which pairing should drive the first action?
workedExamples.reasoning: The strength (strong referrals) paired with the opportunity (open weekday mornings, and local clients who trust referrals) suggests a referral offer aimed at weekday bookings. The threat (discounting) argues against price cuts and for competing on reliability. The owner takes the referral action first and records the response to the discounting separately.

equipmentAndPpe: Evidence log with source and date fields
Competitor list with price band and notes

commonErrors.error: Listing generic items such as 'good service'
commonErrors.prevention: Write each item with a measurable detail or a named source.

commonErrors.error: Putting a threat in the weakness box, or the reverse
commonErrors.prevention: Ask whether the item is within the business's control. If it is not, it belongs in opportunities or threats.

commonErrors.error: Building a long list with no decision at the end
commonErrors.prevention: Rank and pair the items, then choose one action with an owner.
Set a review date at the end of each analysis.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: This lesson gives business planning guidance only. It does not grant any licence, registration or authority to carry out regulated cleaning work.

qualityStandard: Each SWOT item is evidenced or labelled as an assumption.
Each of the top three strengths and weaknesses has a source or a measure.
At least one pairing produces an action with an owner and a review date.
The analysis is dated and reviewed on the set cycle.
documentationEvidence: Dated SWOT analysis with evidence references
Action log with owner, due date and status
Competitor list with price band and source date
summary: A SWOT sorts the situation, and its value lies in the actions it produces.
Strengths and weaknesses need evidence; opportunities and threats need local tests.
Pair items to decide one action at a time.
Review the analysis on a fixed cycle.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which item belongs in the Threats box for a small cleaning business?
options: A trained and experienced team with low turnover
A service area with a fixed radius and a set day
Low overheads from working from home and no rent to pay
Staff leaving because pay and rostering are poor

knowledgeChecks.question: A strength is recorded as 'great team'. What makes it usable?
options: Evidence such as a completion rate, a complaint rate or repeat bookings
Nothing; the entry is already enough and the team already knows it
Adding more positive adjectives and a bigger font for the entry
Moving it into the opportunities box and calling it a sales point

knowledgeChecks.question: Which pairing suggests a protective action rather than a growth action?
options: A strength paired with an opportunity
A weakness paired with a threat
